title: How to Raise an Adult
author: Julie Lythcott-Haims
theme: Children grow into capable, confident adults not when parents clear every path for them, but when parents gradually step back and let them learn to manage their own lives.
summary: Julie Lythcott-Haims spent about a decade as a dean of freshmen at Stanford University, and over those years she noticed something worrying. Many bright, accomplished students seemed unsure how to handle ordinary problems on their own, and some parents were still phoning, emailing and stepping in on their behalf. As a mother, she saw the same habits in her own home.

She describes overparenting as a mix of overprotecting, overdirecting and handholding. Out of love and fear, parents schedule every hour, guard children from all risk, argue with teachers and coaches, and sometimes do homework and applications for them. The goal is usually a safe, successful future, often measured by entry into a small set of prestigious colleges.

The book argues that this approach backfires. Young people who have rarely solved problems, faced disappointment or made their own choices can arrive at adulthood lacking basic life skills and the self-belief that comes from doing hard things. She links this pattern to rising anxiety and low confidence among students, while noting that parents also suffer from the stress of constant management.

Her alternative is practical. Teach everyday skills step by step: first do a task for your child, then do it together, then watch them do it, and finally let them do it alone. Give children real chores, let them talk to adults such as shopkeepers and teachers themselves, and allow plenty of free, unstructured play.

She also urges parents to let children make mistakes and feel the natural results while the stakes are still small, to praise effort and character rather than only grades, and to see that many colleges and many paths can lead to a good life.
Finally, she reminds parents to keep a life of their own. When adults model purpose, rest and resilience, children see what a capable grown-up looks like and feel trusted to become one.
takeaway: This week, pick one task you still do for your child, such as packing a school bag, ordering at a counter or doing a simple chore, and teach it in stages until they can do it on their own.

questions.q: What experience prompted Julie Lythcott-Haims to write How to Raise an Adult?
options: Running a summer camp for teenagers
Working as a family court judge
Serving as a dean of freshmen at Stanford University
Coaching a national sports team
questions.why: Her years as Stanford's dean of freshmen showed her how many students struggled to handle problems on their own.

questions.q: Which three behaviours does the book group together as overparenting?
options: Overprotecting, overdirecting and handholding
Praising, rewarding and punishing
Reading, writing and testing
Ignoring, criticizing and comparing
questions.why: She describes overparenting as a combination of overprotection, overdirection and handholding.

questions.q: According to the book, what usually drives overparenting?
options: A wish to avoid spending time with children
Advice from school principals
Laws requiring parents to supervise homework
Love and fear about a child's safety and future success
questions.why: The author sees overparenting as well-meant, driven by love and anxiety about the child's future.

questions.q: What is the main problem the book sees with constantly clearing a child's path?
options: It makes children too independent too early
It can leave young adults lacking life skills and self-belief
It always leads to poor grades
It makes parents too relaxed
questions.why: Children who rarely solve their own problems miss the chance to build skills and confidence.

questions.q: Which sequence does the book suggest for teaching a child a new skill?
options: Let them try alone, then punish mistakes, then reward success
Explain it once, then expect perfection
Do it for them, do it with them, watch them do it, then let them do it alone
Hire a tutor, then test them, then grade them
questions.why: The gradual handover moves the child from watching to full independence.

questions.q: Why does the author encourage letting children make mistakes while young?
options: The stakes are small, and they learn from natural results
Mistakes guarantee entry to top colleges
Children cannot feel disappointment at a young age
Parents need less involvement once children fail
questions.why: Early, low-stakes mistakes teach lessons that are much costlier to learn later.

questions.q: Which practice does the book recommend for building a child's independence?
options: Speaking to teachers on the child's behalf whenever possible
Filling every free hour with structured classes
Doing chores for the child so they can focus on study
Letting the child talk to adults like shopkeepers and teachers themselves
questions.why: Handling everyday conversations with adults builds practical confidence.

questions.q: What does the book say about college and success?
options: Only a few elite colleges lead to a good life
Many colleges and many paths can lead to a good life
College should be avoided entirely
Parents should choose the child's major
questions.why: She urges parents to look beyond a narrow list of prestigious schools.

questions.q: What kind of praise does the author suggest parents emphasize?
options: Praise only for top marks
Praise for being better than siblings
Praise for effort and character
No praise at all
questions.why: Valuing effort and character helps children see worth beyond grades.

questions.q: Why does the book advise parents to keep a life of their own?
options: So they can spend less money on children
So children see a model of a capable, purposeful adult
So children are left without guidance
So parents can compete with their children
questions.why: Parents who model purpose and resilience show children what adulthood looks like.
